_Bird Study_ (1996) **43,** 124–126

SHORT REPORT

Bird casualties caused by a wind energy project in an estuary

C.J.M. MUSTERS, M.A.W. NOORDERVLIET* _and_ W.J. TER KEURS _Department of Environmental Biology, Leiden University, PO Box 9516, 2300 RA Leiden, The Netherlands_

T he impact of wind turbines on birds in ahigh-risk estuary site was investigated. The area near the Kreekrak sluices is situated near the North Sea coast in the province of Zeeland in the Netherlands; it borders the Oosterschelde, and is used intensively by waders and other water birds.[1] Due to the tidal cycle, there is a great deal of bird movement. Five turbines were installed on the western side of a dike.[2] Each has a capacity of 250 kW, an axis height of 30 m and a three-bladed rotor with a diameter of 25 m; in full action the turbines reach a speed of about 40 rev/min. The distance between the turbines is 125 m. Since 1 April 1990 the turbines have been in action almost continuously. An additional 15 250-kW turbines will be installed if the detrimental effects of this small number of turbines on the bird population prove to be limited in comparison with bird damage caused by the wind turbine plants at other, less risky, locations and if no significant damage to the birds is to be expected. The study also compared the number of casualties among rare birds to those among common birds. Only the effects in terms of collision casualties were studied; the disturbance of the birds by the wind turbines could not be investigated because of the lack of a control area in which changes in bird densities could be studied independently of the installation of wind turbines.

An area of 125 x 125 m around each wind turbine, consisting partly of land and partly of water, was searched for dead birds every other day during the period 28 April 1990 to 29 April 1991. This high searching frequency enabled us to detect even the few corpses that might oth-

*Correspondence author

erwise have been carried off by predators or scavengers. To determine the size of the area, we used Winkelman’s[3] assumption that an area with a radius of 50 m is sufficient to find most, if not all, of the victims of wind turbines. Wherever possible, the cause of death was established.

During this 1-year period, the bodies of 26 birds of 17 different species were found; 6 birds were certainly or almost certainly killed by the turbines. In 3 other cases, the birds may have died because of the turbines, while in the case of 8 birds, it was not possible to determine the cause of death. The remaining 9 birds were not killed by the wind turbines. Table 1 contains an overview of the data for the certain or probable victims of the wind turbines, including their size and the site at which they were found (land or water).

Dead birds are often removed by scavengers, while others may be difficult to find (in the water for instance). Therefore, each month a recovery experiment was carried out to investigate what proportion of a certain number of birds laid out in the area was recovered. The corpses were dropped on land as well as in the water, to compare the chances of finding the birds at different sites. Musters _et al._[2] give more detailed information about the design of this experiment.

It proved much more difficult to recover animals which had fallen into the water than those which had fallen on land. We therefore disregarded the figures on birds found in the water and based our conclusions exclusively on corpses found on land, proceeding on the assumption that the number of birds which fell into the water was identical to the number which came down in a similar section of land in the same area.

On the basis of our experiment, it was estimated that about 98% of the large and medium-sized birds and approximately 73% of the small birds were recovered on land.

All birds were recovered at a constant rate throughout the year: there was no significant difference in the rate of recovery during the various seasons (small birds: ANOVA, _P_ = 0.16, _F_ = 2.182, df = 12; medium-sized and large birds: Kruskal–Wallis test, _P_ = 0.22, _H_ = 4.368, df = 3).

The number of casualties to be expected following the installation of 20 turbines was estimated in two different ways: on the basis of the number of certain victims found, and on the basis of the number of all possible victims (i.e.

the certain, probable and unknown victims in Table 1). The number of bird victims expected during a period of 1 year was estimated at a minimum of 7 and a maximum of 142. This means that the average number of all certain and possible victims amounted to 0.01 per wind turbine per day, with a minimum of 0.006 and a maximum of 0.02 victims per wind turbine per day.

A correlation was found between the number of victims and the estimated number of visitors to the area per species (Spearman Rank correlation: 0.33, _P_ = 0.01, _n_ = 67). This suggests that the rare species among the birds were not excessively endangered by the turbines.

## 126 _Musters, Noordervliet and Ter Keurs_

The number of bird casualties per turbine per day was low in comparison with the results of other Dutch investigations.[5,6] In Oosterbierum (in the province of Friesland) 0.04 probable victims (confidence interval: 0.03–0.11) per turbine per day were recorded during migration in the spring and the autumn. In Urk (in the province of Flevoland) the figure was 0.14 (confidence interval 0.11–0.45). This survey was also carried out during migration in the spring and the autumn.
